# Further reading {#sec-further-reading}

Each chapter ends with a short reading list for that chapter. This page
collects everything in one place, grouped by topic, with a link to the
chapter where each item is most useful. All of it is free to read online
unless marked otherwise.

## Where to start

If you read only three things alongside this book, make it these:

- @clark2003: survival data, censoring and Kaplan–Meier curves, for
  clinicians and researchers (Chapters 1–2).
- @bradburn2003: Cox regression and models with several variables
  (Chapter 3).
- @haukoos2015: a two-page overview of propensity scores and their limits
  (Chapter 5). (May need institutional access.)

## The *British Journal of Cancer* survival analysis series

Four papers from 2003 by the same authors, written for medical researchers.
They make a clear, connected course, and are best read in order.

| Part | Paper | Covers | Goes with |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | @clark2003 | Survival data, censoring, Kaplan–Meier curves, the log-rank test, reporting | Chapters 1–2 |
| II | @bradburn2003 | The Cox model and models with several variables | Chapter 3 |
| III | @bradburn2003b | Choosing a model, and checking its assumptions and fit, including proportional hazards | Chapter 3 |
| IV | @clark2003b | Further topics, including missing data, model validation and repeated events | Beyond this book |

## The *BMJ* Statistics Notes

One-page explanations from Martin Bland and Douglas Altman's long-running
series.

- @bland1998km: the Kaplan–Meier method, with a worked example
  (@sec-km).
- @bland2004logrank: how the log-rank test works (@sec-logrank).

## Hazard ratios and proportional hazards

- @spruance2004: what a hazard ratio does and doesn't tell you, and how it
  relates to probabilities and median survival times (@sec-cox).
- @stensrud2020: why hazard ratios often change over time, and why survival
  curves can be more informative (@sec-ph-check). (May need institutional
  access.)
- @royston2013: *More advanced.* The restricted mean survival time, for
  when hazard ratios aren't constant (@sec-absolute).

## Common traps

- @leung1997: *More advanced.* The kinds of censoring, and why the
  non-informative censoring assumption matters (@sec-informative). (May
  need institutional access.)
- @austin2016cr: competing risks: cumulative incidence, cause-specific and
  Fine–Gray models (@sec-competing).
- @suissa2008: the classic description of immortal time bias, with
  examples from drug studies (@sec-immortal). (May need institutional
  access.)
- @sylvestre2006: the Oscar-winners reanalysis, a short and memorable
  example of immortal time bias (@sec-immortal).

## Propensity scores and matching

- @austin2011intro: the standard introduction to propensity score methods:
  matching, weighting, stratification and checking balance (@sec-psm).
- @stuart2010: *More advanced.* A thorough review of matching methods and
  the choices involved (@sec-matchit).
- @austin2013: estimating and reporting treatment effects on survival after
  propensity score matching, including marginal hazard ratios
  (@sec-together).
- @westreich2013: the Table 2 fallacy: why the other coefficients in an
  adjusted model shouldn't be read as effects (@sec-together).
- @vanderweele2017: the E-value, for judging how strong an unmeasured
  confounder would have to be (@sec-together).

## Weighting and other matching methods

- @chesnaye2022: a short, clear introduction to inverse probability of
  treatment weighting (@sec-weighting).
- @austin2015iptw: best practice for IPTW, including extreme weights and
  survival outcomes (@sec-weighting).

## When proportional hazards fail

- @uno2014: why and how to report the restricted mean survival time
  alongside, or instead of, the hazard ratio (@sec-nonph).
- @royston2013 and @stensrud2020, listed above, are also relevant here.

## Missing data

- @sterne2009: a readable guide to multiple imputation and its pitfalls
  (@sec-missing).
- @white2009: how to include a survival outcome when imputing covariates
  for a Cox model (@sec-missing). (May need institutional access.)
- @vanbuuren2018: a free online book by the author of mice.
- @pishgar2021: matching and weighting after multiple imputation, with the
  MatchThem package (@sec-missing).

## Reporting

- @strobe2007: the STROBE reporting guideline for observational studies,
  with a checklist for writing up (@sec-together).

## Going deeper

- @hernan2020: *Advanced.* A free book on causal inference from
  observational data: confounding, study design and much more.

## R package guides

The guides written by the packages' own authors are the best references for
the code. Each one can also be opened from R with `vignette()`.

- @survival_vignette: the survival package as a whole, especially Cox
  models: `vignette("survival", package = "survival")`.
- @survival_compete: competing risks and multi-state models:
  `vignette("compete", package = "survival")`.
- @survival_timedep: time-dependent covariates, `tmerge()` and landmark
  analysis: `vignette("timedep", package = "survival")`.
- @matchit_vignette: the MatchIt workflow: `vignette("MatchIt")`, and
  `vignette("estimating-effects", package = "MatchIt")` for the analysis
  after matching.
- Greifer N. *Covariate Balance Tables and Plots*: `vignette("cobalt")`.
- @weightit_vignette: the WeightIt workflow: `vignette("WeightIt")`.
- Sjoberg DD et al. *ggsurvfit* documentation:
  <https://www.danieldsjoberg.com/ggsurvfit/>.
- @ucla_survival: free workshop materials on survival analysis in R.
